Chapter 3: Challenging the Traditions That Keep Women Dependent
Picture this: you’re at a family gathering, surrounded by laughter and warmth. The conversation drifts, as it often does, to dreams for the future. When parents talk about their sons, the air is full of excitement—careers, adventures, the thrill of independence. But when their daughters come up? Suddenly, the hopes become quieter. There’s talk of finding a good husband, learning to run a household, and always keeping a cheerful attitude.
It’s subtle, but you can feel the difference, can’t you?
This isn’t just one family—it’s a pattern repeated in homes everywhere. Expectations for women are set by tradition, not logic. From the very start, girls are taught that their value lies in pleasing others, especially men. They’re nudged to be gentle, modest, and agreeable. Don’t rock the boat. Don’t speak too loudly. The unwritten rule? Support, but don’t lead.
Most of us just accept these ideas without even thinking. We’re told that women are naturally meant for a life of dependence, that their happiness is found in submission. But if you pause and really look, it’s clear—these beliefs aren’t rooted in fact. They’re habits, passed down because they’re comfortable, not because they’re right.
And the impact? It runs deep. Women raised to depend on others often struggle to make their own choices. They can be more vulnerable to being manipulated, less able to speak up for themselves. Their lives start revolving around what others want, instead of what they truly need or dream about. This isn’t about nature—it’s learned.
Think about how marriage is framed for young women. It’s often painted as the ultimate prize—the key to happiness and security. Girls are taught to focus on beauty, charm, and obedience. Even their education is shaped to make them appealing, not empowered. What does that lead to? A kind of emotional and intellectual poverty, where a woman’s world is shrink-wrapped by someone else’s expectations.
But not everyone accepts these limits. Some women push back. They choose education, chase their own ambitions, and decide they won’t let relationships define them. It’s not easy—they might face criticism, feel isolated, or even meet outright hostility. But their courage proves something powerful: you can break free from tradition’s grip.
Of course, there’s always resistance. Some folks worry that if women become independent, society itself might unravel. Will families fall apart? Will men lose their place? Will everything just descend into chaos? But here’s the truth—those fears come from misunderstanding what makes people and communities strong. Real stability doesn’t come from keeping women dependent. It grows out of respect and shared responsibility.
When women get the chance to develop their minds and character, everyone wins. They become stronger partners, more engaged parents, and active citizens. They give more to their families and their communities. Equality isn’t just good for women—it benefits us all.
So, let’s be honest. The old traditions that keep women dependent don’t just hold women back—they hold all of us back. They limit what half the world can do, weaken families, and slow progress. If we want a better future, we have to challenge these traditions. We need to build a world where women are truly free—to think, to act, and to shape their own destinies.
